gap: Image A needs a clear directional sun across the whole frame. Every building, and the helicopter, must show distinct lit and shadowed faces, with the shadow side at least about 35% darker. Buildings and trees must cast visible shadows onto streets, rooftops and water. Glass towers and the helicopter body must show specular highlights or sky reflections. The skyline must also fade with distance: towers 3-5 km away should be low-contrast silhouettes tinted toward the sky colour, while the ground within about 500 m keeps full contrast.

Judge: B is clearly better in all three pairs, and no pair is close. B's advantage is the same each time: a clear sun with real light and shadow, strong distance haze that layers the frame in depth, detailed materials with specular response, dense varied ground detail, and cinematic framing. B in pair 1 (backlit banking helicopter) and pair 3 (letters on the hill against a hazy golden skyline) genuinely wow; B in pair 2 is a polished action shot, but its flat midday light keeps it short of a wow. A shows a consistent, recognisable city with good landmark silhouettes, boats with wakes and decent water reflections, but every A frame looks like a scale model. The lighting is flat and ambient with almost no shadows, haze is weak, buildings repeat one window texture, ground planes are flat, trees are clones and there are no people. There are also specific artifacts: blotchy flat rotor-wash foam, golden streaks in the reflections, round blur blobs on the water, and a dark slab cutting into the frame edge. The fixes most likely to close the gap, in order, are directional sun lighting with shadows, a haze gradient with distance, then water spray and wash effects. Two caveats on the protocol. First, the comparison was not truly blind: every B image carries a visible publisher title logo in the corner, so it is obvious which image is the commercial one. Second, the B frames are posed marketing shots with free cameras, while the A frames are gameplay chase-cam captures with the HUD on, so camera and framing are not like-for-like. Neither caveat changes the verdicts, because the lighting, atmosphere and material gaps are large on their own.
